outcome: No proof, disproof, or scope-relevant progress on the conjecture itself was found; the only development since 26 January 2024 is a routine extension of the computational record for the aliquot sequence starting at 276 (to index 2157, exceeding 200 digits, as of November 2025), which per the existence/infinitude scope rule narrows nothing about whether the sequence is truly unbounded and does not count as progress on the conjecture.
summary: The Catalan–Dickson conjecture (every aliquot sequence eventually terminates at a prime-then-1-then-0, or cycles, i.e. no aliquot sequence is unbounded/non-repeating) remains fully open. I searched for proofs, disproofs, partial resolutions (e.g. a proof that some restricted class of starting values must terminate or must diverge), and any AI involvement, and found none. The main line of numerical evidence tracked by the community is the status of the 'Lehmer five' (276, 552, 564, 660, 966), the smallest starting values whose ultimate fate is unknown. The sequence starting at 276 — the most closely watched case — has had its computed trajectory extended further (OEIS A008892 records roughly 2145 terms/214 digits as of its last update, and a search result reports extension to index 2157 / >215 digits as of November 2025 via community computation, e.g. projects tracked at rieselprime.de and FactorDB), but this is a continuation of a decades-long manual/distributed-computing project (using standard integer factorization software), not a change to the mathematical status of the conjecture. Per the deep-dive rules (§3.1), an existence/unboundedness question like this one is not advanced by extending a numerical record further — the record narrows where an answer could hide, not whether the sequence is actually unbounded, so it is correctly excluded from 'progress'. The 2024 Guy–Selfridge counter-conjecture discussion (that aliquot sequences diverge for almost all even seeds) is unchanged background, not a new development. I found no arXiv preprints, journal papers, blog posts (Tao, Quanta, etc.), or lab announcements from 2024–2026 claiming any proof, disproof, or partial theoretical progress (e.g., a proven bound on how many even starting values could plausibly diverge), and no mention of any AI/LLM system being used in this area at all — only traditional distributed/manual computation (factorization software) for extending the 276 sequence. The Wikipedia article on aliquot sequences itself shows no update reflecting new developments beyond the same open-problem framing that existed before January 2024.
competing_reading: One could argue the extension of the 276 sequence to a new record length/index is itself a form of 'progress' worth recording, since it is new computational work performed after the frozen date and is the kind of activity practitioners in this area consider meaningful. I did not classify it as such because the deep-dive rules are explicit that for an unboundedness/existence question, extending how far a sequence has been computed (a record) does not count unless the record IS the question being asked (e.g., 'what is the largest known X') — here the question is whether the sequence is infinite and non-repeating, and no finite amount of extension can answer that.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or heuristic-turned-rigorous argument) that some aliquot sequence is genuinely unbounded (confirming Guy–Selfridge and refuting Catalan–Dickson), or a proof that all aliquot sequences must terminate/cycle (confirming Catalan–Dickson), would settle the conjecture. Short of that, a rigorous theorem establishing that some explicit or provably-existing class of starting values must diverge (even without exhibiting one) would count as genuine progress; a longer computed trajectory for 276 or the other Lehmer-five numbers would not, per the scope rule.
